← Kitchen tile backsplash bid calculator

Do leftover tile boxes cover the laundry wall?

Setters lose money two ways after a kitchen splash: they buy 3.3 boxes on a spreadsheet, or they assume leftover on the van covers the laundry return the owner adds in the driveway. Tile is sold by the box. Waste still applies on the second wall.

Open the kitchen tile calculator, keep your own box size and leftover, and type the laundry or pantry square footage. The table below uses the page defaults: 30 SF subway, 10% waste, 10 SF per box, no leftover on the van.

The 33 SF kitchen buy is four boxes

30 SF of wall with 10% waste is a 33 SF buy. At 10 SF per box that is four boxes (40 SF), not 3.3. You leave the kitchen with 7.0 SF leftover and eat 7.0 SF of round-up on the kitchen ticket.

Wall Need with waste Leftover after kitchen Still buy
Kitchen 30 SF33.0 SF7.0 SF4 boxes
Laundry 8 SF8.8 SFmisses by 1.8 SF1 box
Pantry 6 SF6.6 SFcovers it0 boxes

An 8 SF laundry return with the same 10% waste is 8.8 SF. 7.0 SF leftover misses it. You still buy 1 box. A 6 SF pantry return is 6.6 SF — leftover covers it. Do not buy another box for that return.

Leftover on the van is already-paid stock

Two leftover boxes (20 SF) credit the 33 SF kitchen buy: you still need 13 SF, so you buy 2 boxes, not 4. That leftover does not change the headline installed price unless you decide the van inventory is free. Credit it on materials if you want; leave the labor and extras alone.

Four leftover boxes cover the kitchen without a buy. You still leave 7.0 SF after the splash. Enter the second wall to see whether that leftover is enough.

Open the leftover-box check

This page is a walkthrough of the leftover arithmetic in the kitchen tile backsplash bid calculator. It is not a tile specification, a waterproofing design, a building-code determination, or a price you should copy onto a contract.

Common questions

Do leftover tile boxes cover a laundry or pantry wall?

Not automatically. A 30 SF subway splash with 10% waste is a 33 SF buy. At 10 SF per box that is four boxes, not 3.3, and you leave the kitchen with 7 SF leftover. An 8 SF laundry return with the same waste is 8.8 SF — leftover misses it and you still buy a box.

Why is a 33 SF tile buy four boxes instead of 3.3?

Tile is sold by the box. 33 divided by 10 is 3.3, but you cannot buy three-tenths of a box. Four boxes is 40 SF. You eat 7 SF of round-up on the kitchen ticket whether or not a second wall is on the job.

Does leftover already on the van change the backsplash bid?

Leftover already on the van is already-paid stock unless you decide to credit it. It cuts the boxes you buy next. It does not change the headline installed price by itself.

how-much-to-charge-for-a-kitchen-tile-ba.text:
← Kitchen tile backsplash bid calculator

How much to charge for a kitchen tile backsplash

Tile setters and kitchen remodelers get shopped on a published $35 a square foot installed Facebook special. Those numbers cannot see the pattern or the pull. Thirty square feet of subway running-bond on painted drywall is a different job from 48 SF of herringbone mosaic with eight outlets, a cooktop cutout, Schluter edge, and demo of existing 4x4.

Open the free kitchen tile backsplash bid calculator

Price the wall and the pattern, not the $35 dump

A kitchen backsplash is a wall, then a pattern, then how ready that wall is. Subway running-bond is a stack. Herringbone is cuts and waste. Mosaic is grout. Large-format is leveling. Tile-only sets on a wall that is already ready. New prep is cement board or membrane, then tile. Demo-and-replace is a pull plus the same prep.

Subway versus herringbone on the same wall

Homeowners usually start from the subway special, then ask whether herringbone, mosaic, or large-format is “a little more.” On the same wall and the same scope it is not a little more. Herringbone buys more tile (cuts and waste) and takes a longer set. Mosaic is grout time. Large-format is leveling. The calculator prices all four patterns on the wall you already measured so you can quote the upgrade instead of matching the subway number on a herringbone job.

Tile-only is not a demo-and-replace

The cheap special is almost always subway on painted drywall, two outlets, no cooktop, no Schluter. A herringbone demo is a different crew day. Matching a per-SF number on a demo job is how a sold splash becomes a loss when the cuts and the pull eat the margin.

This is not a shower, a floor, or a countertop

A walk-in shower is a wet area, a slope, and glass. Floor tile is floor waste and tear-out. A quartz or granite countertop is slabs and a sink cutout. Interior painting is a coat. Cabinet refinishing is doors. Drywall is hang and finish gypsum. This prices a kitchen tile backsplash: wall SF, pattern, scope, and extras.

Leftover boxes do not automatically cover the laundry wall

Tile is sold by the box. A 30 SF subway splash with 10% waste is a 33 SF buy. At 10 SF per box that is four boxes, not 3.3, and you leave the kitchen with 7 SF leftover. An 8 SF laundry return with the same waste is 8.8 SF — leftover misses it and you still buy a box. Leftover already on the van is already-paid stock unless you decide to credit it; it does not change the headline bid by itself.

Customer-supplied tile is not a free set

Owners also shop a second special: “I already bought it — just set it for $35 / SF.” Zeroing the tile invoice drops the bid. The trip, the outlet cuts, and the cooktop stay. A short or wrong-lot buy is a second trip. See should I install customer-supplied backsplash tile for the three-way comparison on the same wall.

Saturday is not the weekday bid

A third special is “can you do Saturday so I can cook?” After-hours is time-and-a-half plus a second evening trip. Working around a cook on a weekday is the same wage on a slower set. See should I tile a backsplash after hours for the three-way comparison on the same wall.

Walk-away price

Load the wage with payroll burden. Add overhead as a share of direct cost. Then take margin as a share of the customer’s price, not a markup on cost. The walk-away number is total cost. A proposed price under that number loses money before you take anything out of it.

This page is a walkthrough of the arithmetic in the kitchen tile backsplash bid calculator. It is not a tile specification, a waterproofing design, a building-code determination, or a price you should copy onto a contract.

Common questions

How much should I charge for a kitchen tile backsplash?

Charge from wall square feet, pattern, scope, and extras — not a published $35 / SF special. Thirty square feet of subway running-bond on painted drywall is a different job from 48 SF of herringbone mosaic with eight outlets, a cooktop cutout, Schluter edge, and demo of existing 4x4.

Is tile-only the same bid as a demo-and-replace backsplash?

No. Tile-only sets on a wall that is already ready. New prep is cement board or membrane, then tile. Demo-and-replace is a pull plus the same prep. Matching a per-SF special on a herringbone demo job is how a sold splash becomes a loss when the cuts and the pull eat the margin.

How do herringbone, outlets, and a cooktop change a backsplash price?

Subway running-bond is a stack. Herringbone is cuts and waste. Mosaic is grout. Large-format is leveling. Price all four on the same wall to see the upgrade — matching the subway special on a herringbone job is the losing bid. Outlet cuts, a cooktop cutout, Schluter edge, and an accent band do not live in a published per-SF dump.

Do leftover tile boxes cover a laundry or pantry wall?

Tile is sold by the box. A 33 SF kitchen buy at 10 SF per box is four boxes, not 3.3, and leftover after the splash may still miss an 8 SF laundry return once waste is applied. Leftover already on the van is already-paid stock unless you decide to credit it.

Is this the same as a walk-in shower, floor tile, or a countertop?

No. A walk-in shower is a wet area, a slope, and glass. Floor tile is floor waste and tear-out. A countertop is slabs and a sink cutout. This prices a kitchen tile backsplash: wall SF, pattern, scope, and extras.

← Kitchen tile backsplash bid calculator

Should I install customer-supplied backsplash tile?

Owners call with boxes in the garage: “I already bought the tile. Can you just set it for $35 a square foot?” That sounds like free margin because the tile invoice left the bid. It did not leave the trip, the outlet cuts, the cooktop, or the chance that they bought the measured wall and not the waste — or leftover from another room with a different dye lot.

Open the free kitchen tile backsplash bid calculator

Zeroing the tile is not a free install

A you-supply herringbone still carries the tile invoice. An owner-supplied buy that actually covers zeros that line and keeps the same set hours. On a typical 42 SF herringbone demo — $38 wage, 30% burden, 15% overhead, 20% target margin, 16 miles, six outlets, cooktop, Schluter — the you-supply bid is $3,858.00. Zeroing the tile drops it, but the owner-supplied walk-away stays at $2,698.84. Taking $1,470 ($35 / SF) to “just set what they bought” still loses money.

Short boxes and a wrong dye lot are a second trip

Store shelves and leftover from another room do not include pattern waste. Setting a short or mismatched lot means a callback plus rush tile. Price that on the same splash before you agree. The calculator adds a starting second trip and buys the waste they skipped at a rush multiplier on top of the rates you already typed.

This is not leftover on your van

Leftover boxes already on the van are your stock after a kitchen you bought. That is a different question — see do leftover boxes cover the laundry wall. Customer-supplied tile is their boxes, their lot, and an install-only number. A walk-in shower is a wet area, a slope, and glass. This prices a dry kitchen splash.

How to use the comparison

Open the kitchen tile backsplash bid calculator, pick the herringbone demo preset, and put their install-only number in “price you’re considering.” The who-supplies table scores that number against you-supply, owner-supplies-it-covers, and owner-supplies-short-or-wrong-lot. Nothing is uploaded.

This is the same arithmetic as how much to charge for a kitchen tile backsplash. It is not a tile specification, a waterproofing design, or a reason to refuse a customer — it is the walk-away number on each supply path.

Common questions

Should I install kitchen backsplash tile the customer bought at a store?

Only after you price the set without the tile invoice. Pulling their boxes is still a trip, outlet cuts, and crew hours. A $35 / SF install-only special on a herringbone demo often sits under that walk-away number even when the tile is free to you.

Does customer-supplied tile make the $35 / SF special profitable?

Usually not on the job they actually want. Zeroing a herringbone invoice drops the bid, but loaded labor, travel, outlets, cooktop, and overhead stay. On a typical 42 SF herringbone demo the owner-supplied walk-away is $2,698.84. $1,470 ($35 / SF) still loses money.

What if the store-bought boxes are short or the wrong dye lot?

That is a second dispatch plus rush tile for the waste they skipped. Homeowners buy the measured wall, not the waste, or leftover from another room. Price that callback on the same splash before you agree to set whatever they rolled into the kitchen.

vs-a-flat-rate-per-square-foot.html.text:
← Kitchen Tile Backsplash Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat rate per square foot

“$35 a square foot installed” is not a price for a backsplash — it is a price for one specific pattern, wall condition, and outlet count, quietly applied to every kitchen that calls in.

What a flat rate per square foot is

A flat rate per square foot is the fastest way to quote: multiply the wall's square footage by a number and read off a price. Homeowners shop it because it is easy to compare between bids, and it is the number a homeowner holding a competitor's flyer will ask you to match.

The number behind it was set for one job — subway running-bond on a ready painted wall, tile-only, a couple of outlets — and then reused for every kitchen afterward, whether or not the next wall looks anything like the one the rate was built on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the wall square footage, edge lineal feet, outlets, scope (tile-only, new prep, or demo-and-replace), pattern (subway running-bond, herringbone, mosaic, or large-format), wall condition (painted drywall, cement board, or existing tile), and whether the job needs a cooktop cutout, Schluter edge, or accent band, plus your own labor hours and material costs. It prices the tile, the prep or demo, the wall, and the extras separately, then returns the walk-away price and a bid price above your target margin — for this job, not a generic one.

What a flat rate per square foot doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same $/SF whether the pattern is subway, herringbone, mosaic, or large-format — even though mosaic alone roughly doubles the tile hours per SF and buys more than twice the material of subway running-bond. Prices tile-setting hours and material per pattern (subway, herringbone, mosaic, or large-format), so a mosaic wall is never quoted off a subway rate.
Has no line for the existing tile a demo-and-replace job has to pull first, regardless of whether the wall is ready drywall or a 4x4 tear-out. Prices scope separately — tile-only, new prep, or demo-and-replace — so a job that has to demo and re-prep the wall costs more than tile going straight onto a ready surface.
Prices the wall's measured square footage at one flat number, with no separate line for outlet cuts, a cooktop cutout, Schluter edge, or an accent band. Prices outlets per opening, a cooktop cutout, Schluter edge per lineal foot, and an accent band per SF, so a wall needing all four costs more than a bare wall with none of them.
Applies a single waste percent to every pattern, regardless of how much more a mosaic or herringbone layout leaves on the cutting-room floor. Applies a pattern-specific waste percent to the wall SF before pricing tile material, so a mosaic wall buys more tile than a subway wall on the same footprint.
Gives the setter a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the dollar gap against what a flat rate would have quoted the same job, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

A flat rate is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one wall it was built for, and nothing about a per-square-foot number tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not know your local market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat rate per square foot get a backsplash quote wrong?

Because the cost driver is pattern, wall condition, and extras, not wall area. A mosaic backsplash on existing tile with eight outlets, a cooktop cutout, Schluter edge, and an accent band needs demo hours and dump weight, a much higher tile-setting hours-per-SF and waste rate than subway running-bond, outlet-cut time, and hardware a bare tile-only job on a ready wall never sees. A flat per-square-foot rate charges all of that the same as the cheap special it was built on.

What does a flat rate usually leave out entirely?

Pattern waste, demo, outlet cuts, a cooktop cutout, and Schluter or accent trim. A job that needs the existing tile pulled, eight outlets cut around, a cooktop cutout, edge trim, and an accent band is doing five things a bare tile-only job on a ready wall is not -- and a per-square-foot number has no line for any of them.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped presets: a 30 SF subway-on-painted-drywall special with 2 outlets prices at $1,055.34, which works out to $35.18 a square foot. Applying that same $35.18 rate to a 48 SF mosaic job on existing tile with demo, 8 outlets, a cooktop cutout, Schluter edge, and an accent band quotes $1,688.55 -- $2,516.97 below that job's own $4,205.52 break-even cost, before a dollar of profit, and $3,568.34 below the calculator's own bid price.

Is a flat rate per square foot ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of near-identical jobs -- same pattern, same wall condition, no demo, no cooktop or accent extras either time -- a flat rate can land close. The risk is applying it outside that band without noticing, because the rate does not know which job it was built on and neither does the setter until the wall is actually measured.

Does this calculator know what tile or labor costs in my market?

No. It has no data on local tile invoices or labor rates. It takes the wall square footage, pattern, scope, wall condition, edge length, outlets, cooktop cutout, Schluter edge, accent band, plus the labor hours and material costs you enter, and turns that into a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat rate skips, not a market survey.
